models.title: Taylor rule nominal policy rate (growth-gap variant)
models.summary: Central-bank target nominal rate as neutral real rate plus expected inflation plus half-weight growth and inflation gaps.

relationship.locator: PDF: LM1 Analysis of Monetary and Fiscal Policies, printed p. 39 (PDF p. 49), Taylor rule equation with 6.25% worked example
relationship.translation_notes: Decimal form (unit 1); source works in percentages. The 0.5 weights are the rule's fixed response coefficients (pure arithmetic literals), not conversions. The PDF uses a growth-rate gap (expected vs trend GDP growth); the corroborating Fed statement uses an output-level gap — the 0.5/0.5 response structure is identical. Dimensional check: all terms dimensionless rates.

variables.context: same economy and policy horizon as istar

variables.context: same central bank and policy horizon as istar

variables.definition: Taylor-rule target nominal short-term policy rate, in decimal form
variables.context: same central bank and policy horizon as inputs

assumptions: Policymaker reaction function with fixed 0.5 response coefficients on both gaps, per the source's generic illustration.
Inputs are the central bank's own trend/neutral/expectation judgments, which are not objectively observable (per source).
limitations: Illustrative rule, not a mechanical prescription: substantial judgment remains in every input (per source).
Growth-gap variant as stated in the PDF; level output-gap variants (e.g. the Fed's statement) are companion forms, not separately curated here.

models.title: 120-minus-age heuristic equity allocation
models.summary: Age-based stock allocation heuristic: percentage in stocks equals 120 minus age in years.

relationship.locator: PDF: LM4 Heuristics, printed p. 272 (PDF p. 282)
relationship.translation_notes: Heuristic rule of thumb with no theoretic basis (per source). 120 is the heuristic intercept in percentage points and age is in years; the output reads as a percentage (e.g. 95 means 95%). Both treated as plain counts; no conversion factor is inlined. Dimensional note: heuristic mixes an age count with a percent-points intercept by construction — documented here, not hidden.

variables.context: same investor and allocation decision as weq

variables.definition: Heuristic equity allocation in percent (e.g. 95 means 95% in stocks, remainder in fixed income)
variables.context: same investor and allocation decision as age

assumptions: Application profile: age-driven risk-tolerance glide path; equity share falls linearly with age.
Remainder is implicitly fixed income (per source: age-based stock vs fixed-income split).
limitations: Source explicitly notes no theoretic basis; cousins 100-minus-age and 125-minus-age exist and would be separate records.
May be too conservative for the young (no fixed income needed with emergency fund) and misses sequence-of-returns nuances near retirement (per corroborating source).

models.title: 1/N equal-weight allocation rule
models.summary: Naive diversification: allocate 1/N of wealth to each of N available assets at each rebalancing date.

relationship.original_equation: wi = 1/N for each of N assets
relationship.locator: PDF: LM4 Heuristics, printed p. 276 (PDF p. 286), The 1/N Rule
relationship.translation_notes: wi is the common weight of every asset; N is the count of available assets. Decimal form (unit 1). Dimensional check: dimensionless count reciprocal = dimensionless weight.

variables.definition: Number of assets available for investment at the rebalancing date
variables.context: same investment universe and rebalancing date as wi

variables.definition: Common portfolio weight allocated to each asset
variables.context: same investment universe and rebalancing date as N

assumptions: Calendar rebalancing to equal weighting (e.g. quarterly, per source); all assets treated as indistinguishable in mean, volatility, and correlation.
N is the count of eligible assets at that rebalancing date.
limitations: Sidesteps estimation error but is in principle dominated by optimizations exploiting true return differences (per source empirical discussion).
Equal capital is not equal risk; pair with the risk-parity record, not as a substitute.

models.title: Shrinkage VCV element as weighted average of sample and target
models.summary: Each variance/covariance element of the shrinkage VCV estimate is the same-weighted average of the sample and target matrix elements.

relationship.original_equation: vest = w · vsample + (1 − w) · vtarget (per element, same weights)
relationship.locator: PDF: LM2 Shrinkage Estimation of VCV Matrices, printed p. 109 (PDF p. 119)
relationship.translation_notes: Formalizes the source's prose: each element of the final shrinkage VCV estimate is a weighted average of the corresponding sample and target elements with the same weights on all elements. Decimal form (unit 1); w is the weight on the sample matrix. Dimensional check: dimensionless weight times variance-dimensioned elements = variance-dimensioned estimate.

variables.source_symbol: introduced w for weight on the sample VCV matrix
variables.definition: Weight placed on the sample VCV element (analyst-chosen; 1 − w goes to the target)
Sample variance/covariance matrix element from historical data, in decimal-variance units
variables.context: same asset pair and estimation window as vest

variables.definition: Target (prior-knowledge) VCV matrix element, e.g. from a factor model, in decimal-variance units
variables.context: same asset pair and prior structure as vest

variables.source_symbol: introduced vest for final shrinkage estimate element
variables.definition: Final shrinkage VCV estimate for the element: biased but lower mean-squared error than the sample element
variables.context: same asset pair and estimation as inputs

assumptions: Same weights applied to every element of the matrix (per source).
Application profile: analyst chooses w trading sample noise against target plausibility; a factor-model VCV is a reasonable target candidate (per source).
limitations: Scalar element form only; full-matrix shrinkage with cross-element consistency is outside this record.
Shrinkage is biased by construction; improvement is in mean-squared error, not unbiasedness.

models.inverse_notes: w = (vest − vt)/(vs − vt) requires vs ≠ vt; vs = (vest − (1−w)·vt)/w requires w ≠ 0; vt = (vest − w·vs)/(1−w) requires w ≠ 1. Boundary w=0 (pure target) and w=1 (pure sample) leave one source undetermined. Algebraic only.
